title: “IF I PERISH…”
paragraphs: “IF I PERISH…”
The words weren’t whispered.
They were walked.

Three days without food.
Three nights with only prayer.
No royal makeup could hide the weight in Queen Esther’s chest.
Because the law was clear.
If anyone entered the king’s inner court without being summoned…
Death.

No trial.
No appeal.
Just the sound of guards moving.
And Esther knew it.
She stood outside the throne room doors—robes heavy, crown steady, heart thundering like war drums.
Behind those doors sat the most powerful man in the empire.
Behind her stood an entire people marked for extermination.
Silence.

One step forward…
and her life might end.
But she said it anyway.

“If I perish… I perish.”
—Esther 4:16
Not reckless courage.
Holy courage.
Because Esther understood something many believers forget:

Faith is not the absence of fear.
Faith is obedience in spite of it.
The doors opened.

Marble floors.
Columns rising like giants.
The throne glowing in royal gold.
Every eye turned.
The queen had entered uninvited.
The court froze.

One movement from the king’s hand…
and Esther would die before she spoke a word.
But then—
The king lifted the golden scepter.
Mercy.
Grace in the middle of danger.
Favor where death should have been.
Esther stepped forward and touched the tip of the scepter.

The girl who once hid her identity
now stood before a throne to save a nation.
But this story whispers something even deeper.
Because one day another person would walk toward a throne knowing death awaited.
Not a palace throne.
A wooden cross.
And unlike Esther, Jesus was not spared.
He didn’t say “If I perish.”
He did perish.

For our sin.
For our rebellion.
For every hidden shame we hope no one sees.
Three days later, the King of Heaven raised Him.
Now the throne of God is no longer a place of terror.

Because of Christ, it is a throne of grace.
(Hebrews 4:16)

So when fear tells you to stay silent…
when obedience feels dangerous…
Remember the queen who walked through those doors.
And remember the Savior who walked to the cross.
Courage is not dying for a cause.
Courage is trusting the King with your life.
Someone you know is standing outside a door today, wondering if they should step forward.
Tell them this:

The God who gave Esther courage
is the same God who still moves scepters today.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
